rationale: B wins because it keeps the story inside the four corners of the facts and does not get drunk on Big Tech cosplay. Its best line, "One AI app, two new ways to take a cut," turns the update into a real business-model story without pretending we have numbers we do not. A has good bones, but "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" is exactly the kind of invented competitor frame that gets a founder over-pitched and then ignored.
gaps_in_A: "Putting AI Search Directly Against Google Shopping and Amazon" invents a direct competitive frame the update does not provide. Google and Amazon are plausible calls for context, not facts in the announcement.
"for the first time, an AI search product is inserting itself into the transaction" is an unsupported absolute. One lazy "first" and the whole angle starts smelling like launch copy.
"publishers are already being cited in answers whether or not they join the program" is not in the supplied facts. It may be true, but this judge only gets the update, not vibes.

The publisher counterposition and "It Won't Say How Much" angles are both useful, but they partially cannibalize each other; the opacity angle is strongest as the hard edge of the publisher story unless you can prove rejection or bad terms.
gaps_in_B: "beyond subscriptions" is not in the update. Small overreach, but still an overreach; do not smuggle in business-model context unless the source gives it to you.

"Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting" compresses a messy legal backdrop into a neat reversal. It works as a headline, but the proof burden is high: are the same publishers actually involved?

The set is a little too quick to refuse "The publisher-payout angle: how much will publishers actually earn?" The undisclosed payout is not just proof-it-needs; with a critical media-accountability reporter, the missing number can be the story.
The commerce angle needs one sharper stakeholder: merchant, retailer, affiliate network, or shopper behavior. "shopping surface" is clean, but still a little abstract.
